newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/yen ends tad higher in U.S. on BOJ rate talk.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen ends tad higher in U.S. on BOJ rate talk.

text.p: The dollar closed broadly lower but managed to edge higher versus the yen after reported remarks from a Bank of Japan (BOJ) official and unexpectedly weak industrial production data diminished concern that Japanese interest rates will soon head higher, experts said.

The dollar got a boost during New York trading after a wire service reported that an unnamed BOJ official said the Japanese economic recovery is not strong enough to sustain an interest rate hike, they said.

The Japanese government raised its consumption tax in April. The BOJ official reportedly emphasized that uncertainty about consumer spending was a major factor that made the BOJ reluctant to raise rates.

"This comment here is obviously helping the dollar gain some ground against the yen, and it's also softening the yen on the crosses as well," said Steven Walker, a senior foreign exchange trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in New York.
After the news story hit the wire, the dollar rose back above 116 yen and climbed as high as 116.44 yen in the U.S.
The greenback, however, trimmed its gains to close at 116.25/35 yen, marginally higher than 116.13/23 yen at the opening.

Initially, the dollar strengthened during Asian trading after news of a surprising decline in Japanese industrial production. The Japanese Ministry of International Trade and Industry reported that industrial output in Japan fell a preliminary 0.4 percent in April from the previous month on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected a rise of 0.3 percent to 1.5 percent in April.
Recently, some investors had been concerned the BOJ might soon tighten credit because the economic recovery was strong enough to withstand a small hike in interest rates.
The report on industrial production, however, quieted speculation that a rate increase was right around the corner.
"Personally, I think, the Bank of Japan is not going to be tightening rates as quickly as first thought," said Edith Wolf, head of corporate sales at Credit Commerciale de France in New York.
Wolf said the industrial production data "definitely" led to the dollar pushing above 116 yen.

The dollar/yen rally in New York also helped it trim losses against other currencies including the German mark and Swiss franc. But disappointment that the Swiss National Bank left its discount rate unchanged at a regular weekly meeting of its central bank council and doubts about plans for a single European currency bolstered the Swiss franc.
Switzerland does not plan to join European Economic and Monetary Union, which is scheduled to debut in January 1999.
The Swiss franc is benefitting slightly from the view that it is a safe haven currency in Europe, said Hillel Waxman, a first vice president at Bank Leumi Trust Co in New York.
Uncertainty about the proposed single European currency intensified on Wednesday when the German central bank and government clashed over the government's plans to revalue the bank's gold reserves.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters on Thursday his proposal to revalue the central bank's gold reserves remains necessary despite the bank's strong objection to the plan. He said "not a single mark" from revaluation would be funneled into the government's budget, which critics said would have helped Germany to qualify for inclusion in the single European currency.
The dollar finished at 1.4110/20 Swiss francs and 1.6969/74 marks, down from 1.4148/58 francs and 1.7015/25 marks at the opening.
Sterling rose to $1.6402/12 from $1.6380/90.
The dollar climbed to Canadian $1.3808/13 from C$1.3780/85.
The Australian dollar closed at $0.7655/60, up from $0.7624/29.
-- Donna Sells 212-859-1668
